# manual capture: what a Release build does, emulated on the Debug build
# compiler: main-debug  (<repo>\build\Debug\bin\dxc.exe)
# version:  dxcompiler.dll: 1.10(5433-ab540090)(1.9.0.5433) - 1.9.0.5433 (triage, ab5400907)
# harness:  ndebug-emulate.cmd   (cdb 10.0.26100.6584, x64)  -- re-runnable
# ran:      2026-08-06T22:02:56.4139080-07:00
# NOTE:     hand-driven capture, not a probe. Not scored by match.json.
#           Stacks trimmed to the frames that matter; module-load noise removed.
#
# WHY THIS EXISTS. Every shipping DXC release is a Release build with NDEBUG, where DXASSERT is
# do { } while (0). So "no release binary shows this assert" would be true by construction and
# would say nothing about whether the defect is fixed (SKILL.md, the #2191 trap). The question
# that decides whether the release scan is meaningful is: with the assert gone, does the bad
# state still do damage? Continuing past the assert in the debugger answers it without building
# a Release compiler. This was predicted from source in expected.md BEFORE it was run.
#
# STEP 1 continues past the DXASSERT alone. The very next thing that happens is LLVM's own
#        guard: assert(use_empty() && "Uses remain when a value is destroyed!") in
#        llvm::Value::~Value (lib/IR/Value.cpp:83), reached from BitCastInst::~BitCastInst <-
#        Instruction::eraseFromParent <- TranslateCBAddressUserLegacy. That is the
#        BCI->eraseFromParent() at HLOperationLower.cpp:8845: because the assert arm declined
#        to translate or erase the llvm.memcpy, the bitcast it feeds is destroyed with a live
#        use. In a real Release build this second assert is compiled out as well.
#
# STEP 2 continues past that one too -- the full NDEBUG emulation -- and the compile takes an
#        ACCESS VIOLATION (0xC0000005) in
#           llvm::Type::getTypeID <- Value::stripPointerCasts <- MemTransferInst::getSource
#           <- InstCombiner::visitCallInst <- ... <- InstructionCombiningPass::runOnFunction
#        i.e. InstCombine walks the leftover llvm.memcpy and dereferences its now-dangling
#        source operand. The defect outlives the assert.
#
# CONCLUSION: this is NOT "silent by construction". Whatever the release binaries do on this
# repro is a real measurement, and a clean release would be a genuine fix rather than an
# artefact of NDEBUG.
